messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] web site still down?
messages.body_plain:
It wasn’t a coincidence, but it also wasn’t solely due to the push.

Recall the way DNS works — you enter a domain into a client,
the client finds a local DNS server, asks for what IP that
domain resolves to, and then accesses that IP.  A CNAME
is a redirection at the DNS level —  if a domain has a CNAME
then when a DNS server requests its IP it just forwards the
request to another domain.

So if we want requests for mc-stan.org <http://mc-stan.org> to resolve to github
then we need a CNAME on mc-stan.org <http://mc-stan.org>.  Which is what
I had set up when I went to bed last night, but it takes a long
time for that CNAME to propagate to all of the DNS servers
around the world.  So by the time you pushed most of the
servers were updated and mc-stan.org <http://mc-stan.org> was forwarding as
desired.  When Dan took down the CNAME by restoring
mc-stan.org <http://mc-stan.org>’s DNS settings nothing happened because it
will take a while for those changes to propagate.

Right now you can see the correct behavior,

> dig mc-stan.org <http://mc-stan.org>
…
;; ANSWER SECTION:
mc-stan.org <http://mc-stan.org>.		43200	IN	CNAME	stan-dev.github.io <http://stan-dev.github.io>.
stan-dev.github.io <http://stan-dev.github.io>.	3600	IN	CNAME	github.map.fastly.net <http://github.map.fastly.net>.
github.map.fastly.net <http://github.map.fastly.net>.	15	IN	A	185.31.19.133

You request mc-stan.org <http://mc-stan.org>, the CNAME redirects to
stan-dev.github.io <http://stan-dev.github.io>.  stan-dev.github.io <http://stan-dev.github.io> has its own internal
CNAME that forwards to their custom DNS server that
finally resolves an IP using an alias (hence the A).
Once the CNAME on mc-stan.org <http://mc-stan.org> (i.e. pairNIC) is gone
this will no longer work.

Ido added a CNAME text file to stan-dev.github.io <http://stan-dev.github.io>.  This
doesn’t affect mc-stan.org <http://mc-stan.org> at all.  What it does is it tells
github to treat all of its domains as if they were mc-stan.org <http://mc-stan.org>,
so you can type in stan-dev.github.io <http://stan-dev.github.io> it  will display
“mc-stan.org <http://mc-stan.org>” in your browser window but never contact
the pair servers.

Long story short, I was waiting for the pair CNAME to propagate
to make sure mc-stan.org <http://mc-stan.org> correctly forwarded to github
before adding the CNAME text file back to stan-dev.github.io <http://stan-dev.github.io>.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] web site still down?
messages.body_plain:
I'm sorry, but you're partially mistaken - the CNAME file in GitHub also tells GitHub's web servers when they get an HTTP/1.1 Host: header line with mc-stan.org <http://mc-stan.org> to make that go to the right page (Stan-dev's org page).  Without it, even with the DNS CNAME pointing to Stan-dev.github.io <http://Stan-dev.github.io>, GitHub's web server would display a 404 or 500 error since it doesn't know what page to display when it gets a request for mc-stan.org...

You need both the DNS CNAME and the CNAME file in the org GH page's master branch.  As for DNS propagation delay, even most caching name servers from ISPs respect your DNS refresh time / TTL which you have set reasonably low that the change would be seen within an hour.  You can always check if it's a propagation issue by doing dig mc-Stan.org @ns1.pairwhatever.com <http://ns1.pairwhatever.com> to get a response from Pairnic's/ an authoritative server.  I did this and saw that it was not a DNS issue, it was GitHub not recognizing the Host: header since a CNAME file was missing.

The gh-pages branch in GitHub where you have a CNAME file already is completely ignored by github pages/web servers, but the master branch's CNAME is read and used.

Cheers,
Ido

messages.subject: cloud-stan primer
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

First, I wanted to introduce myself as I'm new to the group. I'm a PhD student at the University of Maryland working in pharmaceuticals (highly aligned with Sebastian's work) and since my thesis/interests revolve around both visualization/application development and deployment I'm going to take a crack at those areas.

Since this group will likely turn into alpha/beta testers a couple things that would be extremely helpful to me are if people could chime in on the following:

a) current/desired dev environment (eg rstudio + shinystan vs r-repl+emacs vs ipython-notebook+pystan etc)

b) project resource consumption - especially upper range of RAM consumption and range of model run times

c) use case - transient (temp environment to be destroyed after logging off) vs day-to-day driver (maintain results/projects/etc).

d) If day-to-day use, what are ideal sync scenarios (dropbox vs github vs direct upload/download, etc)

e) yes/no to desire to ever self-host, and if so hosting platform (internal cluster vs something like AWS).

Thanks and look forward to interacting more with everyone!

Devin

> Hi all,
>
> First, I wanted to introduce myself as I'm new to the group. I'm a PhD student at the University of Maryland working in pharmaceuticals (highly aligned with Sebastian's work) and since my thesis/interests revolve around both visualization/application development and deployment I'm going to take a crack at those areas.
>
> Since this group will likely turn into alpha/beta testers a couple things that would be extremely helpful to me are if people could chime in on the following:
>
> a) current/desired dev environment (eg rstudio + shinystan vs r-repl+emacs vs ipython-notebook+pystan etc)
>
> b) project resource consumption - especially upper range of RAM consumption and range of model run times
>
> c) use case - transient (temp environment to be destroyed after logging off) vs day-to-day driver (maintain results/projects/etc).
>
> d) If day-to-day use, what are ideal sync scenarios (dropbox vs github vs direct upload/download, etc)
>
> e) yes/no to desire to ever self-host, and if so hosting platform (internal cluster vs something like AWS).
>
>
> Thanks and look forward to interacting more with everyone!
>
> Devin
